name: Agreement with the Coeur d'Alene of March 26, 1887, ratified by the Act of March 3, 1891 (Royce 553)
citation: 26 Stat. 989 (Act of March 3, 1891; Royce cites the Coeur d'Alene part at 26 Stat. 1027)
promises: Article 1 recited that the tribe had never ceded its large territory in Washington, Idaho and Montana, that the United States and settlers held it, and that the tribe had received no compensation for it.
Article 2: the tribe ceded all its claim to lands outside its present reservation in Idaho, which it kept.
Article 6: the United States agreed to pay $150,000.
Article 14: the agreement bound neither party until Congress ratified it, which it did on March 3, 1891.

breaches.what: In Article 1 of the agreement Congress ratified in 1891, the United States recited that the Coeur d'Alene had never ceded their lands outside the reservation, that those lands were held by the United States and settlers, and that the tribe had been paid nothing for them.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Agreement of March 26, 1887, Article 1, as quoted in Indian Claims Commission Docket 81, Finding 8 (4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1)

source.title: Coeur d'Alene Tribe v. United States, Docket 81, Findings of Fact (August 26, 1955), 4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

breaches.what: The Commission held that title to the 2,389,924-acre Coeur d'Alene tract passed to the United States on March 3, 1891, that the land was then worth $4,659,663.00, and that the $231,884.97 the United States paid was so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Docket 81, Opinion, Additional Findings and Second Interlocutory Order of December 3, 1957 (6 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, 38)

source.title: Coeur d'Alene Tribe v. United States, Docket 81, Second Interlocutory Order (December 3, 1957)
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

landTaken: 2,389,924 acres in Idaho and Washington, 334,328 of them in Washington (Docket 81 opinion, 1957).
compensation: Paid: $231,884.97 credited by the Commission under Articles 6 and 11. The difference between the value and the payment is $4,427,778.03 (computed for this file from the Commission's two figures; the 1957 orders do not state it). Final award of May 6, 1958: $4,342,778.03, from which attorneys' fees were paid.
today: The Coeur d'Alene Tribe kept its Idaho reservation; the Tribe says its rights to the lower third of Lake Coeur d'Alene were upheld by the Supreme Court in 2001.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the 1873 executive order set its original reservation of more than 500,000 acres, and that the Supreme Court in 2001 upheld its rights to the lower third of Lake Coeur d'Alene.

openQuestions: Audit 2026-11-08: the $4,427,778.03 'found due' figure is not stated in the 1957 opinion, findings or order; it is the value less the payment, now labelled as computed.

The final award amount is read from the 1958 fees order, which names "the award of $4,342,778.03"; the final award document itself was not found in the collection. The 1958 fees opinion's OCR of the same figure is garbled.
The Act of March 3, 1891 also ratified the Coeur d'Alene agreement of September 9, 1889 ceding part of the reservation itself; that cession is not recorded here.
The Tribe's website was cited through cession-1873-11-08-coeur-d-al-ne and not reloaded in this pass.

plain.promised: The Coeur d'Alene kept their Idaho reservation and gave up all other land for $150,000. The United States admitted in the agreement that the tribe had never ceded that land and had been paid nothing.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1957 that the 2,389,924 acres were worth $4,659,663.00 in 1891 and that the $231,884.97 paid was unconscionable.
plain.today: The Commission made a final award of $4,342,778.03 in 1958.
